title: Who Owns a Name
bigQuestion: When nations, federations, founders' heirs and distant schools all claim the same martial art name, what evidence decides who may use it?

story.title: Three Letters on a Door
story.kicker: A lawyer and a teacher read the same sign and see two different things.
paragraphs: A glass door on a small commercial strip carries three letters and a painted emblem. A lawyer for a large federation photographs it. Her client registered those letters and that emblem years ago. She believes the school has no license to use them.

The teacher inside answers with a framed certificate. It shows that her own teacher trained under the founder of the art. To her, the letters name a family of teachers and students, not a company. She says nobody can own a lineage.

Both arguments have a long history. After founders die, their students often split into rival groups that each keep the old name. Federations register marks to protect events and rank systems. Nations list arts as heritage and pass laws naming national sports.

A historian does not pick a side by feeling. She asks for dated records: founding papers, registrations, laws, lecture texts and certificates with numbers. Those records show who used a name first, who changed it, and which institution backs each claim.
story.think: What kind of record would help settle whether the teacher or the federation has the stronger claim to the letters?

lessons.title: Heritage Lists and Stewards
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's 2003 heritage convention lists living traditions with the communities that carry them, which is different from making any state the owner.
reading: On October 17, 2003, UNESCO's General Conference adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage*. It came into force in 2006. The treaty covers living practices such as music, festivals, crafts and games. States that sign it may nominate practices for international lists.

The convention stresses the communities, groups and individuals who keep a practice alive. A state submits the file, but the listing describes the bearers and a plan to protect the practice. A listing does not grant a trademark or a legal monopoly. Other countries remain free to teach and name similar practices.

In November 2018, UNESCO listed traditional Korean wrestling, ssireum, in one entry submitted jointly by North Korea and South Korea. It was the first joint listing by the two states. The file showed that one practice can have more than one *steward*, even across a closed border.

words.d: living practices, such as games, songs and festivals, that communities pass on and that UNESCO's 2003 convention aims to protect
a person, group or state that cares for something on behalf of others without owning it outright
a formal file a state submits asking UNESCO to add a practice to one of its lists

look.title: What the Convention Protects
look.text: The convention defines intangible cultural heritage as practices, expressions, knowledge and skills that communities, groups and sometimes individuals recognize as part of their heritage, passed from generation to generation and constantly recreated.
look.cite: UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Article 2
look.prompt: Whose recognition does this definition put first: a state's, or a community's? Why does that matter for a claim of ownership?

check.q: When did UNESCO adopt its convention on intangible cultural heritage?
check.why: UNESCO's General Conference adopted the convention on October 17, 2003.

check.q: What made the 2018 ssireum listing unusual?
choices: It was UNESCO's first listing of any sport
North and South Korea submitted it together
It gave Korea a trademark on wrestling
check.why: The 2018 ssireum entry was the first joint listing by North Korea and South Korea.

check.q: What does a UNESCO heritage listing NOT do?
choices: Name the communities that carry a practice
Describe a plan to protect a practice
Give one state legal ownership of the practice
Record which state submitted the file
check.why: A listing names bearers and a safeguarding plan; it grants no trademark or monopoly.

lessons.title: A Law Names a National Sport
lessons.mainIdea: In 2018 South Korea amended its taekwondo law to name taekwondo the national sport, turning a cultural claim into a legal one at home.
reading: South Korea passed a law in 2007 to promote taekwondo and build a large taekwondo park. The park, called Taekwondowon, stands in Muju County in North Jeolla Province. It holds training halls, a museum and an arena for events and visitors from abroad.

In 2018 the National Assembly amended the taekwondo law to name taekwondo the country's *national sport*. The change came after years of debate about how to mark the art as Korean. A national sport designation carries weight at home, in schools, budgets and ceremonies. It does not bind other countries or their federations.

The law sits beside international bodies that Korea helped build. Kukkiwon in Seoul issues dan certificates, and World Taekwondo governs the Olympic sport. A *nation brand* works through all three: a domestic law, a national headquarters and a world federation that began in Seoul.

words.d: a sport a government names in law or policy as a symbol of the country
the image a country builds for itself abroad through products, culture and sport
to change a law that already exists

look.title: Two Kinds of Authority
look.text: A South Korean law names taekwondo the national sport. A school in Illinois teaches taekwondo under a license from a federation, and its students test for Kukkiwon certificates. The Illinois school is not bound by Korean law, but it hangs a Korean flag beside the American one.
look.prompt: What authority does the Korean law have over the Illinois school, and why might the school still choose to show the flag?

check.q: What did South Korea's 2018 amendment do?
check.why: The 2018 amendment to the taekwondo law named it South Korea's national sport.

check.q: Where is Taekwondowon?
check.why: Taekwondowon, the park built under the 2007 promotion law, stands in Muju County.

check.q: Which three institutions together make up taekwondo's nation brand in this lesson?
choices: A Korean law, Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo
The Butokukai, the Kodokan and the JKA
Two private schools and a film studio
check.why: The lesson names a domestic law, Kukkiwon's headquarters and the world federation.

lessons.title: Kun Khmer and Muay Thai
lessons.mainIdea: At the 2023 Southeast Asian Games, Cambodia used the name Kun Khmer for a ring event, and a dispute with Thailand showed how a name can carry national pride.
reading: Thailand and Cambodia share a border and a long history of ring fighting with gloves, kicks and elbows. Thailand's version became known worldwide as Muay Thai. Its amateur federation, IFMA, won full IOC recognition in 2021. Cambodia has long called its own ring art *Kun Khmer*.

Cambodia hosted the Southeast Asian Games in Phnom Penh in 2023. As host, it listed the ring event under the name Kun Khmer rather than Muay Thai. Thai officials objected, and Thailand did not send fighters to that event. IFMA, which governs amateur Muaythai, also withdrew its support for the competition.

Each side read the name as a claim about *origin*. Cambodian officials pointed to carvings at Angkor and to Khmer tradition. Thai officials pointed to the sport's modern rules, stadiums and world federation. Historians note that neighboring kingdoms traded soldiers and styles for centuries, so a single birthplace is hard to prove.

words.d: the Cambodian name for Cambodia's ring fighting art
the place or time where something began; often claimed with pride and hard to prove
the country that organizes and runs a set of games, often with power over the event list

look.title: One Ring, Two Names
look.text: A poster for the 2023 Southeast Asian Games lists an event called Kun Khmer. A Thai newspaper headline the same week calls the same ring sport Muay Thai. Both describe gloved bouts in a roped ring with rounds and judges.
look.prompt: What does each name claim about where the sport belongs? What evidence would a historian need before accepting either claim?

check.q: Which country hosted the 2023 Southeast Asian Games?
check.why: Cambodia hosted the 2023 games in Phnom Penh and named the event Kun Khmer.

check.q: How did Thailand respond to the Kun Khmer event name?
choices: It asked UNESCO to cancel the games
It did not send fighters to that event
check.why: Thai officials objected, and Thailand did not send fighters to the Kun Khmer event.

check.q: Why do historians find a single birthplace hard to prove here?
choices: Neighboring kingdoms traded soldiers and styles for centuries
No records of ring fighting exist at all
Both countries use the same language
check.why: Long contact between neighboring kingdoms makes one clean origin hard to document.

lessons.title: A Federation Changes Its Letters
lessons.mainIdea: World governing bodies have renamed themselves many times, which shows that the institution behind a sport's name can change while the sport continues.
reading: A world *federation* is an association of national bodies that writes rules and runs championships. Its name often becomes a set of initials on belts, mats and certificates. Those letters can matter to athletes as much as the sport's own name, because they tell which body stands behind a title.

The World Union of Karatedo Organizations, or WUKO, was founded in 1970. It became the World Karate Federation in 1993. Wrestling's world body, known for decades as FILA, took the name United World Wrestling in 2014. In June 2017 the World Taekwondo Federation shortened its name to World Taekwondo, partly because its old initials had an unwanted meaning online.

In boxing, the International Amateur Boxing Association, AIBA, became the International Boxing Association, IBA, in 2021. A *rebrand* can signal a new start, but records and certificates issued under the old name keep their dates. A historian reading a certificate checks which name the body used in that year.

words.d: an association of national sport bodies that writes shared rules and runs world events
to change an organization's name or emblem to change how the public sees it
the first letters of each word in a name, used as a short form

look.title: When World Bodies Took New Names
look.cite: Official histories of the World Karate Federation, United World Wrestling, World Taekwondo and the International Boxing Association
look.prompt: A certificate reads World Taekwondo Federation. What range of years could it have been issued in, given this chart?

check.q: What did FILA become in 2014?
check.why: Wrestling's world body took the name United World Wrestling in 2014.

check.q: When was WUKO founded?
check.why: The World Union of Karatedo Organizations was founded in 1970 and renamed in 1993.

check.q: Why does a historian check the name a body used in a certain year?
choices: To match a document to the right date and institution
Because renamed bodies erase their records
To find out who won a match
check.why: Certificates keep the name used when they were issued, which helps date and place them.

lessons.title: Recognition Can Be Withdrawn
lessons.mainIdea: The IOC withdrew its recognition of the International Boxing Association in 2023, showing that the right to run an Olympic sport is granted and can be taken away.
reading: The IOC does not own boxing, but it decides which world federation it *recognizes* for the Olympic Games. Recognition gives a federation a seat in the Olympic system and a role in running Olympic events. It also brings a share of Olympic money, which many small federations depend on.

In 2019 the IOC suspended its recognition of AIBA over concerns about governance, finances and the judging of bouts. The IOC ran the boxing events for Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 itself. In June 2023, after the body had renamed itself the IBA, the IOC withdrew recognition entirely. It was the first time the IOC had expelled a world federation this way.

A new body, World Boxing, was founded in 2023 by national federations that wanted Olympic boxing to continue. The IOC granted it recognition in 2025. The sport kept its name through the whole dispute. What changed was which *governing body* could speak for it at the Games.

words.d: for the IOC, to accept a federation officially as the world body for a sport
an organization with the authority to make rules and run official events for a sport
how an organization is run, including its elections, money and decisions

look.title: Same Sport, New Signature
look.text: Two boxing certificates hang in a Chicago gym. One, from 2018, is signed by AIBA officials. The other, from 2025, carries the World Boxing emblem. Both record a boxer's official bouts in the Olympic style.
look.prompt: What changed between the two certificates, and what stayed the same? Who had the power to make that change?

check.q: When did the IOC withdraw its recognition of the IBA?
check.why: The IOC suspended recognition in 2019 and withdrew it entirely in June 2023.

check.q: Who ran Olympic boxing at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024?
check.why: After suspending the federation, the IOC organized the boxing events itself.

check.q: What does IOC recognition give a federation?
choices: A role in the Olympic system and in running Olympic events
Ownership of the sport's name worldwide
check.why: Recognition gives a federation a place in the Olympic system; it does not make it the owner of the sport.

lessons.title: Aikido's Many Houses
lessons.mainIdea: Aikido's founder left one foundation in Tokyo, but his leading students built separate organizations that all teach under the aikido name.
reading: Ueshiba Morihei, born in 1883, created aikido from older Japanese jujutsu and sword traditions. A foundation to support his teaching was set up in 1940. In 1948 it was reorganized as the Aikikai Foundation, based in Tokyo. Leadership of the Aikikai has passed within the Ueshiba family, from Morihei to his son Kisshōmaru and grandson Moriteru.

Senior students also built their own houses. Shioda Gōzō founded the Yoshinkan in 1955. Tomiki Kenji developed a version with competition. In 1974 Tōhei Kōichi, once the Aikikai's chief instructor, left and founded the Ki Society. Each group issues its own ranks and certificates.

None of these groups owns the word aikido in every country. Each claims *authenticity* through a documented link to Ueshiba, such as years of study or rank he awarded. A historian compares those links with dated records. The *schism* shows how one founder can leave several legitimate heirs.

words.d: the quality of being genuine; in martial arts, a claim to teach what a founder taught
a split of one organization into rival groups
a legally registered organization set up to support a purpose, such as teaching an art

look.title: Aikido Groups by Founding Year
look.cite: Aikikai Foundation official history; Yoshinkan and Ki Society official histories
look.prompt: Which group was founded while Ueshiba was still alive, and which after his death? Why might that matter to each group's claim?

check.q: Who founded the Ki Society in 1974?
check.why: Tōhei Kōichi, the Aikikai's former chief instructor, founded the Ki Society in 1974.

check.q: What is a schism?
choices: A split of one organization into rival groups
check.why: A schism is a split into rival groups, as happened in aikido.

check.q: How does each aikido group support its claim?
choices: By a documented link to Ueshiba
By owning the word aikido worldwide
check.why: Each group points to recorded study or rank from Ueshiba.

lessons.title: Two Taekwondo Federations
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo split between the International Taekwon-Do Federation and the body now called World Taekwondo, and each issues its own ranks and runs its own events.
reading: General Choi Hong-hi founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation, the ITF, in Seoul in 1966. In 1972 he left South Korea after conflict with its government and moved the ITF abroad. The next year, South Korea's national association helped found the World Taekwondo Federation in Seoul.

The two bodies grew apart. They used different forms, different competition rules and different rank certificates. World Taekwondo's version entered the Olympics. The ITF version spread through Choi's network of instructors, and from the 1980s it was also taught in North Korea.

Choi died in 2002 in Pyongyang. After his death, rival leaders each claimed to head the ITF, and several groups still use the name. A student's *certificate* therefore names not just an art but a *federation*. The paper tells a historian which branch of a divided family the student belongs to.

words.d: the International Taekwon-Do Federation, founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966
an official paper that records a rank and the body that granted it
one part of a group that has divided from a shared beginning

look.title: Two Black Belt Papers
look.text: A family keeps two taekwondo black belt certificates from the 1990s. One carries the ITF emblem and Choi Hong-hi's signature. The other is a Kukkiwon certificate with a registration number, linked to World Taekwondo. Both holders say they study taekwondo.
look.prompt: Are both certificates real taekwondo ranks? What does each one tell you about the institution that stands behind it?

check.q: Where did Choi Hong-hi die in 2002?
check.why: Choi died in Pyongyang in 2002, after which rival ITF groups formed.

check.q: Which version of taekwondo entered the Olympics?
check.why: The Olympic sport follows the rules of World Taekwondo.

check.q: Why did Choi move the ITF out of South Korea?
choices: He was invited by the IOC
He left after conflict with the South Korean government
check.why: Choi left South Korea in 1972 after conflict with its government.

lessons.title: Kyokushin Splits
lessons.mainIdea: After Kyokushin karate's founder died in 1994, rival groups each claimed his organization and its name.
reading: Ōyama Masutatsu founded *Kyokushin* karate in Tokyo and set up its international organization in 1964. His style became known for full-contact tournaments. By the 1980s, Kyokushin had branches in many countries. Ōyama himself remained the single head of the whole organization.

Ōyama died in April 1994. He left no successor that every senior student accepted. Within a few years, the organization divided into several groups. Each claimed to be the true Kyokushin and used the name, the emblem, or both. Some disputes reached Japanese courts and trademark offices.

Today several international Kyokushin bodies hold separate tournaments and grant separate ranks. A student's belt means most inside the group that awarded it. The story shows how a *succession* dispute turns one founder's legacy into competing claims.

words.d: a karate style founded by Ōyama Masutatsu, known for full-contact tournaments
the process of choosing who takes over a role after a leader dies or leaves
what a person leaves behind, including an organization, a name and students

look.title: Two Tournaments, One Name
look.text: In the same year, two tournaments in different cities both call themselves the Kyokushin world championship. Each hangs Ōyama's portrait above the stage. Each issues its winners a certificate with a different emblem.
look.prompt: What would you ask each organizer to prove that its claim to the Kyokushin name is stronger?

check.q: When did Ōyama Masutatsu die?
check.why: Ōyama died in April 1994, and his organization soon divided.

check.q: What is a succession dispute?
choices: A disagreement over the rules of a match
A disagreement over who takes over after a leader
check.why: Succession is choosing who takes over; Kyokushin split when no successor was accepted by all.

check.q: Where does a Kyokushin belt carry the most meaning today?
choices: Inside the group that awarded it
check.why: Separate Kyokushin bodies grant separate ranks.

lessons.title: Tang Soo Do Keeps Its Name
lessons.mainIdea: Hwang Kee's Moo Duk Kwan kept the name Tang Soo Do rather than join taekwondo, and American service members carried that name to the United States.
reading: Hwang Kee founded the Moo Duk Kwan in Seoul in 1945, soon after Korea's liberation from Japanese rule. He called his art *Tang Soo Do*. The name uses characters that can be read as way of the Tang hand, pointing to China. The same characters are read karate-dō in Japanese.

In the 1960s, many Korean kwan joined the new national taekwondo association. Hwang Kee kept his school and his name apart from that merger. So Tang Soo Do continued as a separate art in Korea, with its own ranks and rules. A later branch of the Moo Duk Kwan did join the taekwondo association, so the kwan name itself came to have two meanings.

American service members stationed in Korea studied at Korean schools in the 1950s and 1960s. One was Chuck Norris, who learned Tang Soo Do while serving in the U.S. Air Force. Returning soldiers opened schools in the United States. Many American Tang Soo Do *diaspora* schools still trace their lineage to Korea rather than to a U.S. federation.

words.d: a Korean art name used by Hwang Kee's Moo Duk Kwan; the characters match the Japanese karate-dō
people or institutions spread far from their homeland who keep ties to it
the joining of separate organizations into one

look.title: Characters Read Two Ways
look.text: A school sign shows three Chinese characters. A Korean teacher reads them as Tang Soo Do. A Japanese teacher reads the same characters as karate-dō. An American student sees only the English words painted beneath.
look.prompt: What does this sign show about how a written name can travel across languages and still point to different histories?

check.q: Who founded the Moo Duk Kwan in 1945?
check.why: Hwang Kee founded the Moo Duk Kwan in Seoul in 1945.

check.q: Why is Tang Soo Do still a separate name?
choices: Hwang Kee kept his school out of the taekwondo merger
The U.S. Air Force invented it
check.why: Hwang Kee stayed apart from the 1960s taekwondo association.

check.q: How did Tang Soo Do reach the United States?
choices: Through American service members who trained in Korea
check.why: Service members such as Chuck Norris trained in Korea and opened schools at home.

lessons.title: Judo in Japanese Brazil
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese immigrants who reached Brazil from 1908 built judo clubs, and Brazilian judo later won Olympic medals under the Brazilian flag.
reading: In June 1908 the ship Kasato Maru reached the port of Santos carrying the first organized group of Japanese *immigrants* to Brazil. Most came to work on coffee farms. Over the next decades, more families followed. The state of São Paulo became home to one of the largest Japanese communities outside Japan.

Immigrant communities built schools, newspapers and sports clubs. Judo clubs were among them, often led by teachers trained in Japan. For many families, judo kept a tie to Japanese language and custom. Over time, the clubs opened their doors to Brazilians of every background.

Brazilian judo then entered the Olympic record. Chiaki Ishii, born in Japan, won bronze for Brazil at the 1972 Munich Games. Aurélio Miguel won Brazil's first judo gold in Seoul in 1988, and Rogério Sampaio won gold in Barcelona in 1992. The medals show a diaspora art becoming part of a new *national* sport culture.

words.d: a person who moves to a new country to live there
belonging to a whole country, such as a team that represents it
a club run by and for a local group, often an immigrant group

look.title: A Club Photograph
look.text: A photograph from São Paulo shows a judo club's members lined up in white jackets. A sign above them is written in Japanese. Decades later, a photograph of the same club shows a Portuguese sign and a Brazilian flag on the wall.
look.prompt: What changed between the two photographs, and what do the changes suggest about who the club served?

check.q: What arrived at Santos in June 1908?
choices: The Kasato Maru with Japanese immigrants
check.why: The Kasato Maru carried the first organized group of Japanese immigrants to Brazil in 1908.

check.q: Who won Brazil's first Olympic judo gold medal?
check.why: Aurélio Miguel won Brazil's first judo gold at Seoul in 1988.

check.q: What did judo clubs often mean to Japanese Brazilian families?
choices: A tie to Japanese language and custom
check.why: The clubs helped families keep ties to Japanese language and custom.

lessons.title: A Founder's Own Words
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō's 1889 lecture on judo is a dated record of what he said judo was for, which gives historians evidence stronger than later legend.
reading: Claims about a martial art's name are strongest when they rest on dated *primary sources*. For judo, one of the most useful is a lecture Kanō Jigorō gave in Tokyo in 1889. He spoke to an education society, seven years after opening the Kodokan in 1882.

In the lecture, Kanō explained why he chose the word judo instead of jujutsu. He described three aims for his school: physical education, contest and moral training. He also argued that judo belonged in Japan's schools. The text was printed, so later readers can check exactly what he claimed.

At least one older jujutsu school had used the word judo before Kanō. What made Kanō's judo distinct was its institution: a named hall, a rank system and published aims. A historian weighing ownership looks for this kind of *evidence*. A dated lecture tells more than a story told decades later.

words.d: a record made at the time by someone involved, such as a lecture text, law or letter
facts or records that support or weaken a claim
a family of older Japanese unarmed fighting schools from which Kanō built judo

look.title: Kanō's Three Aims
look.text: Kanō told his audience that judo had three purposes: to train the body, to prepare for contest, and to cultivate the mind and character. He argued that its methods could be used in ordinary life, not only in the practice hall.
look.cite: Kanō Jigorō, lecture on judo and its educational value, Tokyo, 1889
look.prompt: How could this dated lecture help settle an argument about what judo meant to its founder?

check.q: When did Kanō give his lecture on judo's aims?
check.why: Kanō gave the lecture in Tokyo in 1889, seven years after founding the Kodokan.

check.q: Which three aims did Kanō describe?
choices: Physical education, contest and moral training
check.why: The lecture named physical education, contest and moral training.

check.q: Why is a dated lecture strong evidence?
choices: It was made at the time and can be checked
It was written by a film studio
It proves no one used the word before
check.why: A primary source from the time lets readers check what was actually said.

review.q: What does a UNESCO intangible heritage listing record?
choices: The communities that carry a practice and a plan to protect it
review.why: The 2003 convention centers the bearers and a safeguarding plan, not ownership.

review.q: Which name did Cambodia use for its ring event at the 2023 Southeast Asian Games?
review.why: As host, Cambodia listed the event as Kun Khmer.

review.q: What happened to the IOC's recognition of the IBA in 2023?
choices: It was granted for the first time
review.why: The IOC withdrew its recognition of the IBA in June 2023.

review.q: Which statement best compares the aikido and Kyokushin splits?
choices: In both, several groups kept the founder's art name
Both were settled by the IOC
review.why: Both arts ended with several groups using the same name after their founders.

review.q: What did South Korea's 2018 amendment change?
choices: It named taekwondo the national sport
It created the Moo Duk Kwan
review.why: The 2018 amendment named taekwondo South Korea's national sport.

review.q: Why did Tang Soo Do stay a separate name in Korea?
choices: Hwang Kee kept his school out of the taekwondo merger
review.why: Hwang Kee did not join the 1960s national taekwondo association.

review.q: Which is a primary source for judo's aims?
choices: A rumor told at a tournament
review.why: Kanō's printed 1889 lecture was made at the time by the founder.

review.q: Who won bronze in judo for Brazil at the 1972 Olympics?
review.why: Chiaki Ishii, born in Japan, won Brazil's bronze at Munich in 1972.
